classification.difficultyReason: Use the semi-vertical angle to eliminate radius, then follow supplied derivative targets to calculate height and base-area rates and reverse the volume-rate calculation.

content.prompt: Sand being poured from a conveyor belt forms a cone with height $h$ and semi-vertical angle $60^\circ$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that the volume of the pile is $V=\pi h^3$, and differentiate with respect to $t$.

answer.worked:
Let $r$ be the radius of the base. From the semi-vertical angle,
$$\begin{aligned}\tan60^\circ&=\frac rh=\sqrt3\\r&=h\sqrt3.\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}V&=\frac13\pi r^2h\\V&=\frac13\pi(3h^2)h\\V&=\pi h^3.\end{aligned}$$
Differentiating with respect to $t$,
$$\frac{dV}{dt}=3\pi h^2\frac{dh}{dt}.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Suppose that the sand is being poured at a constant rate of $0.3\text{ m}^3/\text{min}$, and let $A$ be the area of the base. Find the rate at which the height is increasing:

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that $\displaystyle\frac{dA}{dt}=6\pi h\frac{dh}{dt}$, and find the rate of increase of the base area at these times.

answer.short: $\displaystyle\frac{dA}{dt}=6\pi h\frac{dh}{dt}$. At $h=4\text{ m}$: $\frac3{20}\text{ m}^2/\text{min}$; at $r=4\text{ m}$: $\frac{3\sqrt3}{20}\text{ m}^2/\text{min}$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\pi r^2\\A&=3\pi h^2\\\frac{dA}{dt}&=6\pi h\frac{dh}{dt}.\end{aligned}$$
At the time in part b(i),
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dA}{dt}&=6\pi(4)\frac1{160\pi}\\\frac{dA}{dt}&=\frac3{20}\text{ m}^2/\text{min}.\end{aligned}$$
At the time in part b(ii),
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dA}{dt}&=6\pi\left(\frac4{\sqrt3}\right)\frac3{160\pi}\\\frac{dA}{dt}&=\frac{3\sqrt3}{20}\text{ m}^2/\text{min}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: At what rate must the sand be poured if it is required that the height increase at $8\text{ cm/min}$, when the height is $4$ metres?

answer.worked:
Use $h=4\text{ m}$ and $\frac{dh}{dt}=8\text{ cm/min}=0.08\text{ m/min}$.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dV}{dt}&=3\pi h^2\frac{dh}{dt}\\\frac{dV}{dt}&=3\pi(16)(0.08)\\\frac{dV}{dt}&=3.84\pi\text{ m}^3/\text{min}.\end{aligned}$$
